title: Inferences rest on the text
statement: An inference, modelled or asked for, may combine only what the text shows with what every student can be assumed to know, never an outside cultural or world fact.
detail: A ruling in the reading project struck a worked example whose extension reached for outside-world knowledge of a foreign city that the course's students could not be expected to have: an inference may only use what the passage's own words show, and an extension deepens the mood from remaining text clues, never a civic or cultural fact the passage never gave (`grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/knowledge/kb-0180-lesson-structure-procedure-rulings.qmd`). The same procedure's frame is "The text says ___, and I know ___, so I think ___", so the knowledge an inference may add is what every student can be assumed to have.
against: the same procedure defines inference as combining text clues with what you know (the same file), so where assumed knowledge ends and an outside fact begins is a judgment. The project's own inference frame combines text clues with what the student knows, so where allowed background ends and an outside fact begins is a judgment (`grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/knowledge/kb-0180-lesson-structure-procedure-rulings.qmd`, line 76).

Three hard rules on the frame, from the authored designs:
The "I know that" move supplies WORLD knowledge (what anyone knows about being trapped, being tired, wanting to be safe), never a second quote and never a fact the text already states.
A modelled inference may only use what the passage's own words show, so the extension deepens the mood from the remaining clues instead of adding a civic "rules" layer.

London-mood, flying-mood, and Neverland-mood inferences all require either lesson-supplied knowledge bridges (Step 3 MCQ/MSQ at each release level) or common-sense prior knowledge (cold/dark, feather-in-wind)
A model think-aloud reasons only from passage evidence, never from background knowledge the child cannot be expected to have.
